source.title: Data Augmentation Revisited: Rethinking the Distribution Gap between Clean and Augmented Data
source.authors: Z. He; Ling-Xi Xie; Xin Chen; Ya Zhang; Yan-Feng Wang; Qi Tian

record.file_problem: Full paper text supplied. Some table rows are flattened, and blank refinement cells are not recoverable from the supplied text.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports its own image-classification results on natural labels, measuring how intensive data augmentation and a clean-data refinement stage affect training and test losses or accuracy. This is a related test of generalization behavior, but it does not test the specific versions listed.
record.gate_note: Rows cover the paper's own reported outcomes for augmented training followed by refinement. Cited prior-work results and theoretical claims are not rows. The paper reports additional table and figure results; the extracted rows prioritize accuracy comparisons and clean-versus-augmented training loss. Flattened or missing table entries were not reconstructed.
record.test_reason: The study tests augmentation and refinement schedules, which none of V1–V8 names. It does not compare random versus natural labels, widths beyond interpolation, convolutional versus fully connected networks, optimizers, batch sizes, dropout interventions, magnitude-aware sharpness, or removal of memorized examples. Using dropout in one recipe does not test V6.
record.authors_conclusion: The record captures the authors' conclusion: they argue that intensive augmentation improves generalization while leaving higher clean-data empirical risk, and that late refinement with less intensive augmentation can reduce that risk and improve classification and detection transfer. The proposed better-region mechanism is an interpretation supported by their analysis and observations, rather than a directly established causal result. Their broad improvement language also has exceptions in the reported results.
record.recipe_differences: The study changes data augmentation during training and adds a clean or standard-augmentation refinement stage; it does not reproduce a listed version's intervention.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcome varies with dataset, model, augmentation method, whether standard augmentation is retained during refinement, and refinement schedule. The paper reports a CIFAR10 accuracy drop for standard augmentation refined without augmentation, while CIFAR100 improves; Shake-Shake with Cutmix on CIFAR10 also drops slightly. ImageNet results vary by model and augmentation.

fits_no_version.finding: Removing intensive augmentation late in training often improves image-classification accuracy. For example, PreActResNet-18 on CIFAR100 improves from 78.95% to 80.85% after Mixup and from 79.33% to 80.09% after AutoAugment.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Late refinement with less intensive augmentation can improve image-classification accuracy, depending on the model, dataset, and augmentation recipe.

fits_no_version.finding: The study measures differences between clean and augmented training losses and their changes after refinement; these are not magnitude-aware sharpness measurements.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Intensive augmentation can leave a distribution gap between clean and augmented training losses, and refinement can lower clean-training loss.

fits_no_version.finding: Section 4.4 reports that refinement of Mixup- and AutoAugment-pretrained backbones improves detection mAP beyond both their unrefined counterparts and the original backbone.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Refining intensively augmented classification backbones can improve their transfer to object detection.

record.problems: Some reported accuracy results are means over three independent experiments, but no uncertainty values are supplied in the tables. The source text flattens some tables, obscuring model-to-value assignments; those ambiguous cells are marked accordingly. No random-label control or capability check is reported.
record.rows_left_out: Additional Tiny-ImageNet results (Table 4), the fixed-total-epoch Mixup-removal sweep (Figure 4), and most ImageNet Top-5 results (Table 5) were not extracted. Figure 4 values are figure-only in the supplied text; Table 4 and additional Table 5 cells were omitted to prioritize clearer accuracy comparisons within the row limit.

untested.parts: Coexistence of random-label fitting and natural-label generalization, including chance-level random-label test accuracy.
Test error as width increases beyond the width needed for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected networks and the contribution of local connectivity or initialization.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizers, tuning breadth, decoupled weight decay, and optimizer switching.
Large versus small batches under matched epoch budgets and recipe adaptations.
Dropout interventions, training-set-size dependence, excessive dropout, and joint removal of dropout and weight decay.
Magnitude-aware weight-perturbation sharpness, its association with generalization gaps, and comparison with alternative measures.
Retraining after removing highly memorized versus randomly selected examples.

record.verdict_notes: All row states are cannot_determine relative to V1–V8 because their measurements address no listed version; this does not mean their numerical augmentation effects are unreadable. These own-method comparisons should be excluded from the claim-evidence rows and retained as fits_no_version findings. Several flattened-table corrections depend on omitted Standard refinement cells; the surrounding prose supports that ordering for ImageNet and detection. No claim-relevant missing results were identified.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and held-out performance on natural versus random labels.
Width sweeps beyond the interpolation threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected architectures and local connectivity.
Adaptive versus non-adaptive optimizers and tuning or optimizer changes.
Large versus small batch sizes under fixed epoch budgets.
Dropout-specific effects and its interaction with removing weight decay.
Magnitude-aware sharpness or comparisons with norm- and margin-based measures.
Removing memorized training examples and measuring resulting test accuracy.
